intro: Vladimir de Pachmann recorded two Chopin pieces on this side of HMV DB 860 in 1925: the Étude in F major, Op. 25 No. 3, followed by the Waltz in C♯ minor, Op. 64 No. 2. Pachmann, born in 1848, made the recording by the new electrical process.

sections.label: A · Étude in F major
sections.mNote: Four piano voices move in a galloping rhythm.

sections.label: B · Étude in F major continued
sections.mNote: The quick sideways leaps in both hands continue.

sections.label: C · Waltz in C♯ minor
sections.mNote: Held melody notes above a three-beat accompaniment.

sections.label: D · Waltz melody and running quavers
sections.mNote: The right hand alternates the melody with quick descending phrases.

sections.label: E · Waltz, closing chords in C♯ minor

cues.title: Étude Op. 25 No. 3 before the Waltz
cues.text: The first piece is Chopin’s F major Étude, Op. 25 No. 3. Its hands jump sideways while four voices share the galloping rhythm. Pachmann puts it before the C♯ minor Waltz on a single HMV record side.
cues.evidence: Programme order: https://archive.org/details/hmv-db860-chopin-nocturne-no8-op27no2-etudes-op25no3-waltz-no7-op64no2. Étude’s four voices and lateral hand movements: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Étude_Op._25,_No._3_(Chopin)

cues.title: Electrical recording sessions, Hayes, 1925
cues.text: At Hayes on 26 June 1925, Pachmann recorded for HMV on his own Baldwin. These sessions produced the company’s first electrical solo-piano recordings. In The Gramophone that December, the critic K. K. complained about the new sound but welcomed one improvement: “he does not utter a word the whole time.”
cues.evidence: Session and instrument documentation, quoting K. K., The Gramophone, December 1925, pp. 338–39: https://archive.org/details/hmv-db860-chopin-nocturne-no8-op27no2-etudes-op25no3-waltz-no7-op64no2

cues.title: Opening of the C♯ minor Waltz
cues.text: The C♯ minor Waltz begins with a melody in paired notes, held across the bar line. Short turning figures follow it, over a bass note and two chords in the left hand. The four voices of the Étude are followed by three beats in the bar.
cues.evidence: Waltz opening, Knute Snortum engraving (2023), p. 1. The established section boundary marks the change of work. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/2/28/IMSLP879636-PMLP2373-waltz-op64-no2.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Pachmann’s recital programme, Yale
cues.text: On stage, Pachmann talked before playing and sometimes while playing. The surviving programme of his all-Chopin recital at the Yale School of Music, which is undated, announced his Baldwin piano. Its inside cover carried an advertisement for Steinway.
cues.evidence: Yale School of Music’s surviving programme and account of Pachmann’s stage manner: https://music.yale.edu/2009/04/03/from-the-archives-vladimir-de-pachmanns-all-chopin-recital-at-the-yale-school-of-music. The programme itself is undated.

cues.title: Final cadence in C♯ minor
cues.text: The waltz’s running tune continues to the end. Its descending quavers reach the cadence in C♯ minor, which ends both the second piece and the record side.
cues.evidence: Score, final Più mosso and cadence, p. 5. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/2/28/IMSLP879636-PMLP2373-waltz-op64-no2.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

composer.born: 1 March 1810, Żelazowa Wola, Duchy of Warsaw
composer.epithet: Composer for the piano, known for music that drew on operatic singing and on the irregular accents of the mazurka.
facts: Wojciech Żywny; composition with Józef Elsner in Warsaw, 1826–29
Warsaw · Paris from 1831 · summers at Nohant
Piano lessons, publishing and occasional concerts
The piano, from a few lines of mazurka to concertos and sonatas
composer.background:
In February 1832 Chopin, a twenty-one-year-old Polish pianist, played in the Pleyel rooms in Paris. He had arrived the previous autumn, with two concertos behind him. The concert caught the attention of the city’s publishers, and teaching soon supplied his living. For the rest of his life his profession depended on people hearing him at close quarters. The great public virtuosos travelled from one concert city to the next; Chopin stayed in Paris and gave lessons.

He was born at Żelazowa Wola in 1810. His father, Nicolas, had come from France and worked as a tutor; his mother, Justyna Krzyżanowska, was Polish. The family moved to Warsaw while Fryderyk was still a baby, when Nicolas obtained a teaching post at the Lyceum. At seven the boy had a polonaise in print. Wojciech Żywny taught him the piano, with Bach and Mozart among his models; Józef Elsner later gave him a rigorous training in composition at Warsaw’s Main School of Music.
